\# Introduction

\# Diamonds Descriptive Statistics

\## Length

```{{r}}
library(tidyverse)
data(diamonds)

newDiamonds <- diamonds |>
  filter(x != 0, y != 0, z != 0) |>
  select(color, x, y, z)

# Calculate length statistics by color
length_table <- newDiamonds |>
  group_by(color) |>
  summarise(
    Frequency = n(),
    `0%` = quantile(x, 0),
    `20%` = quantile(x, 0.20),
    `40%` = quantile(x, 0.40),
    `60%` = quantile(x, 0.60),
    `80%` = quantile(x, 0.80),
    `100%` = quantile(x, 1),
    Median = median(x),
    Mean = mean(x),
    `Sample SD` = sd(x),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

knitr::kable(
  length_table,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Descriptive Statistics for Diamond Length by Color"
)
```

\# Big Ten Academic Alliance

```{{r}}

library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

# Import the datasets
teams <- read_csv("~/Downloads/teams.csv")
team_box <- read_csv("~/Downloads/team_box (1).csv")

# Identify Big Ten teams
big_ten <- teams |>
  filter(conference_name == "Big Ten Conference")

# Calculate average points for each Big Ten team
team_averages <- team_box |>
  filter(team_id %in% big_ten$team_id) |>
  group_by(team_display_name) |>
  summarise(
    average_points = mean(team_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Create the visualization
ggplot(
  team_averages,
  aes(
    x = reorder(team_display_name, average_points),
    y = average_points
  )
) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Average Points Scored by Big Ten Women's Basketball Teams",
    x = "Team",
    y = "Average Points per Game",
    caption = "Source: Big Ten women's basketball team statistics"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

\# Monte Carlo Numerical Integration

```{{r}}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# Function to generate random points
monte_carlo <- function(n, x_min, x_max, y_min, y_max) {
  x <- runif(n, min = x_min, max = x_max)
  y <- runif(n, min = y_min, max = y_max)
  data.frame(x = x, y = y)
}

# Assigned function: Beta(2, 2) density
# Exact integral from 0 to 1 is 1

# Create plots using different numbers of random points
make_mc_plot <- function(n) {
  points <- monte_carlo(n, 0, 1, 0, 1.5)

  points$flag <- ifelse(
    points$y > dbeta(points$x, shape1 = 2, shape2 = 2),
    "above",
    "on/below"
  )

  p <- mean(points$flag == "on/below")
  estimate <- p * 1.5

  ggplot(points, aes(x = x, y = y, color = flag)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 0.7) +
    stat_function(
      fun = dbeta,
      args = list(shape1 = 2, shape2 = 2),
      color = "blue",
      linewidth = 1
    ) +
    scale_color_manual(
      values = c("above" = "red", "on/below" = "green")
    ) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1.5)) +
    labs(
      title = paste("n =", n, "| Estimate =", round(estimate, 4)),
      x = "x",
      y = "y",
      color = "Point Location"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
}

# Four simulation sizes
make_mc_plot(100)
make_mc_plot(500)
make_mc_plot(1000)
make_mc_plot(5000)

\# Planning and Prompting GenAI Tools

\## My Plan

I plan to compare how ulna calcium measurements changed over the four years for the null treatment group and the diet and exercise group. Since the data is currently separated into different columns for each group and year, I will first organize it into a longer format. I will include variables for the group, year, and calcium measurement. I will then create a line graph showing the average calcium measurements over time for both groups. I will also check for missing values before analyzing the data.

\## Plan-Informed GenAI Response

Based on your plan, I would first convert the calcium dataset from wide format into long format so that each observation has a group, year, and calcium measurement. This will make it easier to compare the null treatment group with the diet and exercise group.

I would then check for missing values and keep them as `NA` rather than replacing them with zero. When calculating the average calcium measurements for each group and year, I would use `na.rm = TRUE` to exclude missing values.

Finally, I would create a line graph with year on the x-axis, average calcium measurements on the y-axis, and separate lines for each group. This would make it easier to see how the measurements changed over the four years and compare the patterns between the groups.

\## Generic GenAI Response

I would first examine the calcium dataset and organize it into a long format so that each row represents one participant's calcium measurement at a specific time point. I would identify the treatment group and measurement year for each value, making it easier to compare the two groups.

Next, I would check for missing values and leave them as `NA` rather than replacing them with zero. I would use `na.rm = TRUE` when calculating the averages so that missing values are excluded from the calculations.

I would then calculate the average ulna calcium measurement for each group at each time point. Finally, I would create a line graph with the measurement year on the x-axis, average calcium measurement on the y-axis, and a separate line for each treatment group.

A line graph would be useful because it shows how the average measurements change over time and makes it easier to compare the null treatment group with the diet and exercise group.

\## Comparison

The plan informed response followed the steps I originally wanted to take, while the generic response came up with its own approach. Both responses organized the data and suggested a line graph to compare the groups. This showed me that giving GenAI a plan can help it produce results that better match what I am looking for.

\# Appendix B: Code

Diamonds Challenge:

```         

#Load packages and data
library(tidyverse)
data(diamonds)

#Remove diamonds with zero dimensions
newDiamonds <- diamonds |>
  filter(x != 0, y != 0, z != 0) |>
  select(cut, x, y, z)

#Put x, y, and z into one column
diamondsLong <- newDiamonds |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = x:z,
    names_to = "Dimension",
    values_to = "Value"
  )

#Calculate statistics for each cut and dimension
statVals <- diamondsLong |>
  group_by(cut, Dimension) |>
  summarise(
    Count = length(Value),
    Min = min(Value),
    Q1 = quantile(Value, 0.25),
    Median = median(Value),
    Q3 = quantile(Value, 0.75),
    Max = max(Value),
    MAD = mad(Value),
    Mean = mean(Value),
    SD = sd(Value),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

#View the results
statVals
```

Diamonds Table of Descriptive Statistics:

```         
# Step 1: Load Packages and Data ----
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

data(diamonds)

# Step 2: Select the Needed Data ----
diamondsDepth <- diamonds |>
  select(color, z)

# Step 3: Calculate Descriptive Statistics ----
diamondsStats <- diamondsDepth |>
  group_by(color) |>
  summarize(
    Count = n(),
    Min = min(z),
    Q1 = quantile(z, probs = 0.25),
    Q2 = quantile(z, probs = 0.50),
    Median = median(z),
    Q3 = quantile(z, probs = 0.75),
    Q4 = quantile(z, probs = 1),
    Max = max(z),
    Mean = mean(z),
    SD = sd(z),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Step 4: Format the Table ----
diamondsTable <- diamondsStats |>
  rename(
    Color = color,
    `Sample Minimum` = Min,
    `First Quartile` = Q1,
    `Second Quartile` = Q2,
    `Sample Median` = Median,
    `Third Quartile` = Q3,
    `Fourth Quartile` = Q4,
    `Sample Maximum` = Max,
    `Sample Arithmetic Mean` = Mean,
    `Sample Arithmetic Standard Deviation` = SD
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(
      where(is.numeric) & !any_of("Count"),
      \(x) round(x, 2)
    )
  )

# Step 5: Display the Final Table ----
diamondsTable |>
  kable(
    caption = "Descriptive Statistics for Diamond Depth by Color",
    digits = 2
  ) |>
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
    full_width = FALSE
  )
```

```         
# Big Ten Women's Basketball Data Wrangling

# Load packages
library(readr)
library(dplyr)

# Import datasets
teams <- read_csv(
  "teams.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

games <- read_csv(
  "games.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

rankings <- read_csv(
  "rankings.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

team_box <- read_csv(
  "team_box.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Extract and import player box scores
zip_file <- "game_box (1)-compressed.zip"

player_file <- "game_box.csv"

extract_folder <- tempdir()

unzip(
  zip_file,
  files = player_file,
  exdir = extract_folder,
  overwrite = TRUE
)

player_box <- read_csv(
  file.path(extract_folder, player_file),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Identify Big Ten teams
big_ten_teams <- teams |>
  filter(conference_name == "Big Ten Conference") |>
  distinct(team_id, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  select(
    team_id,
    team,
    display_name,
    abbreviation,
    conference_name,
    conference_short_name
  )

# Create a list of Big Ten team IDs
big_ten_team_ids <- big_ten_teams$team_id

# Filter games involving at least one Big Ten team
big_ten_games <- games |>
  filter(
    home_id %in% big_ten_team_ids |
      away_id %in% big_ten_team_ids
  )

# Filter team box scores to Big Ten teams
big_ten_team_box <- team_box |>
  filter(team_id %in% big_ten_team_ids) |>
  left_join(
    big_ten_teams |>
      select(
        team_id,
        conference_name,
        conference_short_name
      ),
    by = "team_id"
  )

# Filter player box scores to Big Ten teams
big_ten_player_box <- player_box |>
  filter(team_id %in% big_ten_team_ids) |>
  left_join(
    big_ten_teams |>
      select(
        team_id,
        conference_name,
        conference_short_name
      ),
    by = "team_id"
  )

# Filter rankings to Big Ten teams
big_ten_rankings <- rankings |>
  filter(team_id %in% big_ten_team_ids) |>
  left_join(
    big_ten_teams |>
      select(
        team_id,
        conference_name,
        conference_short_name
      ),
    by = "team_id"
  )

Monte Carlo Numerical integration:

```         
library(ggplot2) 

# Function to generate random coordinates
monte_carlo <- function(n, x_min, x_max, y_min, y_max) {
  
  x <- runif(n, min = x_min, max = x_max)
  y <- runif(n, min = y_min, max = y_max)
  
  data.frame(x = x, y = y)
}

# Define the function
f <- function(x) {
  -(x - 4)^2 + 4
}

# Define sample sizes
sample_sizes <- c(10, 100, 1000, 10000)

# Generate points and classify them
results <- lapply(sample_sizes, function(n) {
  
  points <- monte_carlo(n, 2, 6, 0, 4)
  
  points$flag <- ifelse(points$y > f(points$x),
                        "above", "on/below")
  
  # Calculate the estimated integral
  p <- mean(points$flag == "on/below")
  estimate <- p * 16
  
  points$n <- n
  points$estimate <- estimate
  points$plot_label <- paste0(
    "n = ", n, "\nEstimate = ", round(estimate, 4)
  )
  
  points
})

# Combine all results
all_points <- do.call(rbind, results)

# Create the four small multiple plots
ggplot(all_points, aes(x = x, y = y, color = flag)) +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_function(fun = f, color = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~plot_label, ncol = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("above" = "red", "on/below" = "green")
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(2, 6), ylim = c(0, 4)) +
  labs(
    title = "Monte Carlo Integration Example",
    x = "x",
    y = "y",
    color = "flag"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
  
  library(ggplot2)

# Generate 1000 random points
points <- monte_carlo(1000, 0, 1, 0, 1.5)

# Classify points as above or on/below the function
points$flag <- ifelse(
  points$y > dbeta(points$x, shape1 = 2, shape2 = 2),
  "above",
  "on/below"
)

# Calculate the estimated integral
p <- mean(points$flag == "on/below")
estimate <- p * 1.5

# Create the plot
ggplot(points, aes(x = x, y = y, color = flag)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  stat_function(
    fun = dbeta,
    args = list(shape1 = 2, shape2 = 2),
    xlim = c(0, 1),
    color = "blue",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("above" = "red", "on/below" = "green")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = paste("Monte Carlo Integration, Estimate =", round(estimate, 4)),
    x = "x",
    y = "y",
    color = "Point Location"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1.5)) +
  theme_minimal()

# Display estimated integral
estimate
```

Calcium Dataset:

```         
library(tidyverse)

# Import calcium dataset
calcium <- read_csv("calcium.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Rename columns
names(calcium) <- c(
  "null_y0", "null_y1", "null_y2", "null_y3",
  "diet_y0", "diet_y1", "diet_y2", "diet_y3"
)

# Convert data from wide format to long format
calcium_long <- calcium |>
  mutate(participant = row_number()) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -participant,
    names_to = c("group", "year"),
    names_pattern = "(null|diet)_y(\\d)",
    values_to = "calcium"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    group = recode(
      group,
      "null" = "Null Treatment",
      "diet" = "Diet and Exercise"
    ),
    year = as.integer(year)
  )

# Check for missing values
sum(is.na(calcium_long$calcium))

# Calculate average calcium measurements
calcium_summary <- calcium_long |>
  group_by(group, year) |>
  summarise(
    average_calcium = mean(calcium, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Create line graph
ggplot(
  calcium_summary,
  aes(x = year, y = average_calcium, color = group, group = group)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = 0:3,
    labels = c("Initial", "Year 1", "Year 2", "Year 3")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Changes in Ulna Calcium Measurements Over Four Years",
    x = "Measurement Year",
    y = "Average Ulna Calcium",
    color = "Treatment Group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
